title: Holiness is given
hook: Luzzatto's last rung: after effort, holiness comes as a gift

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was step by step: zeal, cleanliness, separation, purity, the middle rungs of the ladder. Which habit did you refine? Today, the rung at the top. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

A seed goes into the ground on a spring morning. The gardener did the digging, the watering and the weeding, and she will keep doing them. But no gardener can pull a sprout up out of the dirt by hand. At some point the work stops being hers, and something else happens on its own time. Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto spent a whole book on hard, careful work: watchfulness, zeal, cleanliness, the rungs we've been climbing. Then, on the last rung, he says something that sounds almost like a gardener. Today, the top of the ladder, and the surprise waiting there.
screen: `A SEED IN THE GROUND.` → `THE WORK, THEN THE WAITING.` → `THE TOP OF THE LADDER.`

segments.voice: Luzzatto's book is called The Path of the Just. Its ladder comes from an older saying in the Talmud, in the name of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair: Torah leads to watchfulness, watchfulness to zeal, and so on up, through purity, piety, humility and the fear of sin, until the saying reaches holiness. Turn that last rung four ways. First, the command. Holiness isn't a word Luzzatto made up. The Torah says, in Leviticus: "Ye shall be holy; for I the LORD your God am holy." It is spoken to a whole people, not to a few saints. Second, the twist. Luzzatto writes that holiness has two parts. Its beginning is effort: a person works to set themselves apart for God, in thought and in deed. Its end is a gift: God, he says, grants the holiness that effort alone could never finish. The climb is yours; the summit is given. Third, the source. Luzzatto leans on a line from the Talmud, in tractate Yoma: a person who makes himself a little holy below is made much holy from above. A little, then much. The proportion is the point. Fourth, what it looks like. For Luzzatto, the holy person doesn't leave ordinary life. He describes even eating and working, for such a person, as acts that serve God, the way an offering on the altar did. Holiness here is not a cloud above the kitchen; it is the kitchen, lifted. So the last rung is a strange kind of rung. Every step below it asked for more effort. This one asks for effort, and then for open hands.
screen: `A LADDER FROM THE TALMUD.` · `YE SHALL BE HOLY.` · `EFFORT FIRST, THEN A GIFT.` · `A LITTLE BELOW, MUCH FROM ABOVE.` · then, large: `HOLINESS IS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: aim high, then let go. Sit comfortably and breathe. Let one high aim come to mind, something you'd like your life to hold: more patience, more honesty, a gentler home, a deeper prayer. Hold it clearly for a few breaths. Now name the one small step that is truly yours to take today. See yourself taking it. Then, on an out-breath, open your hands on your knees. Whatever comes of the step is not yours to force. If you pray, you can hand the rest over in your own words. If you don't, simply rest with your hands open. The bell holds the time.
Holiness is given. In Hebrew, kedushah: holiness, the last rung of Luzzatto's ladder, begun by effort and finished as a gift. Today's word.
Your line: holiness is given. Today, take your one small step fully, and then leave the outcome open. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Students of Mussar often read The Path of the Just slowly, a chapter at a time, sometimes aloud with a study partner, working on each trait in turn; its closing chapters on holiness are read as the goal the whole ladder points toward.

trapdoor: what you thought: holiness is something you earn by being very good.
what it means: holiness starts with a person's effort to set themselves apart, and is finished as a gift.
what a scholar hears: The Path of the Just builds on Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's ladder, and leans on Yoma's line: a little holy below, much holy from above.
